god.note: Luke ends his list "the son of God," so Jesus’ line is tied to all humanity and not only to Israel.

seth.note: Born to Adam and Eve after Abel’s death (Genesis 4:25).

enoch.note: He walked with God and was taken by God without dying (Genesis 5:24).

methuselah.note: The longest life in Scripture, 969 years (Genesis 5:27).

noah.note: Built the ark and survived the flood (Genesis 6–9).

cainan-2.note: Some Hebrew texts of Genesis 11 do not have this name; the Greek Old Testament does. This is one reason the lists are hard to compare name for name.

eber.note: Some think the word "Hebrew" comes from his name.

terah.note: Abraham’s father, who set out from Ur toward Canaan (Genesis 11:27–32).

abraham.note: God promised him a land, many descendants, and that all nations would be blessed through him (Genesis 12). Matthew starts here.

jacob-1.note: Renamed Israel; his twelve sons became the tribes (Genesis 32; 35).

judah-1.note: Jacob’s fourth son. Jacob’s blessing says the scepter will not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10).

perez.note: Matthew says "Perez and Zerah by Tamar." Genesis 38 tells the story.

w.note: Judah’s daughter-in-law. Her story is in Genesis 38. Perez and Zerah were her sons by Judah.

ram.note: Ruth 4:19 and 1 Chronicles 2 also have Ram.

arni.note: Luke has two names (Admin, Arni) where Matthew has one (Ram). Some manuscripts of Luke differ here too.

nahshon.note: Leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness (Numbers 1:7; 2:3).

w.note: Matthew says Boaz was her son. Many take her to be Rahab of Jericho, who hid the spies (Joshua 2, 6); the Bible does not say so outright.

obed.note: The son of Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 4:17).

w.note: A Moabite widow who stayed with her mother-in-law Naomi and married Boaz. The book of Ruth tells her story.

jesse.note: David’s father in Bethlehem. Isaiah 11:1 speaks of "a shoot from the stump of Jesse."

david.note: King of Israel. God promised him a son whose throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7), the promise the Gospels see fulfilled in Jesus.

solomon.note: David’s son who built the temple in Jerusalem.

w.note: Matthew does not use her name, only "Uriah’s wife." She was David’s wife, and the mother of Solomon (2 Samuel 11–12).

rehoboam.note: Under his rule the kingdom split in two (1 Kings 12).

joram.note: Matthew skips three kings between Joram and Uzziah (Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah; 1 Chronicles 3:11–12). "Father of" here means "ancestor of," which helps Matthew keep his pattern of fourteen.

hezekiah.note: The reforming king in the days of Isaiah (2 Kings 18–20).

manasseh.note: Judah’s longest-reigning and most wicked king, who repented late in life (2 Chronicles 33).

josiah.note: The king who found the Book of the Law and led a great reform (2 Kings 22–23). Matthew leaves out Jehoiakim between Josiah and Jeconiah.

jeconiah.note: Taken to Babylon in the first exile, about 597 BC (2 Kings 24). Matthew starts his third set of fourteen with him.

nathan.note: A son of David and Bathsheba (2 Samuel 5:14). He is not the prophet Nathan.

shealtiel.note: Matthew makes him the son of Jeconiah and Luke the son of Neri; this is where the two lists meet again.

zerubbabel.note: Led the first return from Babylon and rebuilt the temple (Ezra 3; Haggai 1–2).

abiud.note: From here Matthew names men who are not named elsewhere in Scripture.

jacob-2.note: In Matthew, Joseph’s father. In Luke, Joseph’s father is Heli.

heli.note: Luke says Jesus was "regarded as the son of Joseph, the son of Heli." Matthew calls Joseph’s father Jacob. Common explanations: one list gives Joseph’s legal line and the other his birth line, or one follows Mary’s family. The Gospels do not say which.

joseph.note: Mary’s husband, from Nazareth. Matthew 13:55 calls Jesus “the carpenter’s son.” Both lists end with him, but Matthew says Jesus was "born" of Mary and Luke says Jesus was "regarded as" Joseph’s son.

w.note: Matthew calls Joseph "the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus." Both Gospels say Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit.

jesus.note: "Who is called Christ" (Matthew 1:16). Matthew’s list proves a royal line from David; Luke’s shows a Savior for everyone, back to Adam and God.

segs.s: Only Luke goes back this far

segs.t: David to the exile in Babylon
segs.s: The lists divide: Solomon in Matthew, Nathan in Luke

intro.m: Matthew starts with Abraham and moves forward to Jesus. He arranges the names in three sets of fourteen (Abraham to David, David to the exile, the exile to the Christ), possibly because the letters of David’s name add up to fourteen in Hebrew. He includes four women besides Mary, and leaves out a few kings.
intro.l: Luke starts with Jesus and moves backward, past Abraham to Adam and to God. His list is much longer and includes no women. It comes right after Jesus’ baptism, when the voice from heaven calls him "my beloved Son."
intro.why: From David on, the two lists share almost no names until Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, and then divide again before Joseph. The Gospels do not explain this. Common explanations are that one list traces Joseph’s legal line and the other his birth line, or that one follows Mary’s family. Matthew writes for readers who care that Jesus is the Son of David; Luke for readers who need to know he belongs to all people.
